claims.text: A machine-learning model trained on high-throughput phonon-transport data and local structural descriptors will predict low phonon thermal conductivity in high-entropy alloys more accurately than existing semi-empirical or first-principles methods.
The target materials are near-equiatomic high-entropy alloys in a disordered solid-solution state.
Such disordered, near-equiatomic HEAs are typical of thermal-insulation applications at elevated temperatures.
The proposed model will be trained on experimental phonon thermal-conductivity data spanning multiple HEA compositions and temperatures.
The model will incorporate local chemical complexity, lattice distortion, and predicted phonon-scattering descriptors.
The approach is applicable within the composition and temperature ranges represented in its training data.
The intended temperature range extends to several hundred degrees Celsius.
Phonon scattering is the dominant thermal-transport mechanism under the intended conditions.
Local chemical disorder and lattice-distortion metrics capture relevant atomic-scale interactions.
Local chemical disorder and lattice-distortion metrics capture phonon-scattering processes.
Machine learning will learn complex nonlinear correlations between the chemical and structural descriptors and measured thermal conductivity.
Learning these correlations will account for compositional and disorder-induced scattering effects that traditional models miss.
Existing rules-of-mixtures and first-principles baselines do not comprehensively incorporate local disorder and complex multielement interactions.
The proposed model will improve prediction accuracy by approximately 20–30% relative to the baseline models.
Predictive accuracy may diminish for phase-transforming compositions, disorder outside the training domain, and temperatures where additional heat-conduction mechanisms become significant.
The magnitude of the accuracy improvement depends on the quality and breadth of the experimental training set and on descriptor selection.
High-throughput computational screening combined with experimental validation can accelerate HEA materials discovery.
The model will be benchmarked by synthesizing predicted low-conductivity HEAs, measuring their thermal conductivity, and comparing model errors against conventional methods.
Failure to achieve a statistically significant improvement of at least 20% in prediction error within the stated domain will falsify the hypothesis.
